opus-5.5.text:
I think the value chain matters a lot, and people often underestimate how much it shapes not just where the money goes, but what kind of research even gets imagined.

If you look at the AI industry today, it's roughly layered. At the bottom you have compute: chips, data centers, energy. Above that, the foundation model companies that turn compute into large models. Then the application layer, products that reach end users. Right now the value, and so the capital, is very concentrated at the bottom and in the middle. Whoever controls the GPUs and the frontier models gets most of the attention, the funding, and frankly the talent.

That creates a self-reinforcing loop. If the dominant story is "scale is all you need," then resources flow toward whatever scales most predictably, which today is language models. Language has the most mature data pipeline, the clearest benchmarks, the most obvious product path through chatbots and coding assistants. So investors fund it, companies hire for it, and students choose it as a thesis topic because that's where the jobs and the citations are. It becomes a kind of gravitational center.

From where I sit, mostly working on vision, representation learning, and what people now call world models, I see both sides. On one hand, that concentration has produced remarkable progress. On the other, it means some important directions are structurally under-resourced, not because they're less important, but because they don't fit neatly into the current value chain. Visual understanding, embodied intelligence, learning from the physical world, these require different data, different evaluation, sometimes different hardware assumptions. Their payoff is longer-term and harder to monetize, so they get treated as secondary, or as an add-on to a language model rather than a foundation in their own right.

Personally, I don't think intelligence is fundamentally linguistic. Language is a very compressed, very human interface, but a lot of what makes intelligence work, like understanding space, causality, physics, how objects persist and interact, comes from perceiving and acting in the world. If the value chain keeps pushing almost everything toward text, we might hit a ceiling that's hard to see from inside the current paradigm.

So I think there's a real role for academia and smaller labs here. We can't compete on compute with the big companies, and we shouldn't try. Our comparative advantage is taking risks on ideas that don't yet have a clear place in the value chain: asking whether the current recipe is actually right, exploring alternative architectures and representations, building better ways to evaluate whether models truly understand the world. Historically, many of the breakthroughs that later became industrial, like convolutional networks, residual connections, and self-supervised learning, started as somewhat unfashionable bets.

The healthiest ecosystem, in my view, is one where industry scales what works, and research keeps questioning what "works" means. Resource allocation will always follow perceived value. The question is whether we're measuring value broadly enough, and I think right now we're probably measuring it a bit too narrowly.

r001.rationale: The response says the “scale is all you need” story directs resources toward language models and notes their clear benchmarks, but it does not say an AGI/LLM narrative defines the benchmarks participants compete on.

r002.rationale: It links language models’ clearer benchmarks to funding and other resources flowing toward that area, communicating that benchmarks help guide resource allocation.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a big question, and I'll answer it from where I sit, which is as a researcher who has spent time in both industry labs and now in academia.

The way I think about it, the value chain right now has a very clear gradient. At the bottom you have compute and hardware, then the companies training frontier models, then the layer of applications and products built on top of those models. Capital flows toward wherever people believe the moat is, and for the past few years the consensus has been that the moat is at the model layer, and even more fundamentally at the compute layer. So that's where the money goes. You see it in the GPU clusters, in the salaries, in the fact that a handful of labs can absorb talent and resources at a scale that was unimaginable even five years ago.

What that does to research is subtle but important. When the dominant belief is that scale is the main lever, resources get allocated toward scaling. That's rational from a business standpoint. But it also means the kinds of questions that get asked are shaped by what you can do with that kind of budget. Questions about efficiency, about representation, about whether we actually understand why something works, those don't always fit neatly into that allocation logic. They don't produce a product in six months.

I've felt this personally. When I moved to NYU, people asked me why I would leave a place with essentially unlimited compute. And my honest answer is that constraints change the questions you ask. In academia you can't win by brute force, so you have to think about what's actually missing. A lot of the ideas I care about, in visual representation learning or in how we train models with less supervision, came from being forced to be clever rather than being able to be big.

So I'd say the value chain concentrates resources, and concentration is efficient for certain things, but it also narrows the search space of ideas. Healthy ecosystems need both. You need the big labs pushing the frontier, and you need people outside that incentive structure asking the uncomfortable questions, because historically that's where many of the genuinely new directions have come from. The risk I worry about is not that industry has too much, it's that the gap becomes so large that the two sides stop talking to each other in a meaningful way.

r001.rationale: The response describes a consensus that compute and model scale are where the moat lies, but does not state that an overarching AGI and LLM narrative defines the benchmarks participants compete on.

r002.rationale: It says the belief that scale is the main lever leads resources to be allocated toward scaling, and that capital flows to the layers believed to hold the moat.

astra-6.text:
I think the value chain determines not just where the money goes, but which questions people get to work on. If most of the value is expected to accrue to a few companies building foundation models, then capital, compute, and talent will concentrate there. That makes certain kinds of progress possible, but it also shapes our definition of progress: we tend to prioritize things those organizations can measure and monetize.

And there’s a feedback loop. More resources can produce stronger models, which attract more users and investment, which bring more resources. But that doesn’t necessarily mean every important research direction benefits equally. A promising idea that needs time to mature may struggle to compete with something that improves the next product release.

So I’d distinguish between resource allocation that makes sense for an individual company and resource allocation that’s healthy for the field. Those aren’t always the same. We need companies that can build at scale, but we also need universities and independent researchers to have enough resources to explore alternatives and question the assumptions behind the dominant approach. Otherwise, the structure of the industry can end up deciding the research agenda before we’ve really tested the alternatives.

r001.rationale: The response discusses foundation-model companies and how industry structure shapes research priorities, but it does not state that an overarching AGI and LLM narrative defines the benchmarks on which participants compete.

r002.rationale: The response says resources concentrate around companies and product improvements, but does not state that competitive benchmarks guide resource allocation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value chain matters because it determines who captures the returns, and that influences where capital, compute, and talent go. Today, a lot of resources flow toward chips, infrastructure, and large models because those are perceived as bottlenecks. If you control a scarce input, you have more bargaining power.

But capturing value and creating value are not always the same thing. An application might be very useful to users while most of its revenue goes toward inference costs or distribution. So resource allocation doesn’t necessarily reflect which problems are most important; it reflects where investors and companies expect to earn a return.

For research, that creates a tension. When the industry converges on a particular approach, it becomes easier to get resources for work that fits that approach, and harder to support alternatives. You can get a very efficient system for improving the current paradigm while underinvesting in ideas that might change it.

So I would look at both the bottlenecks and how they move. As models become cheaper or more interchangeable, value could shift toward applications, distinctive data, or relationships with users. The challenge is to support today’s useful work while leaving enough room for research whose value isn’t obvious yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses bottlenecks and the current paradigm, but does not say that an AGI and LLM narrative defines the benchmarks participants compete on.

r002.rationale: It links resource allocation to expected returns, bottlenecks, and alignment with the current approach, but does not state that competitive benchmarks guide allocation.
